content.content: Let $f:\S^2\to \S^2$ be a branched cover, $V(f)$ be the set of its critical values,  and $A, B\subset \S^2$ be  finite sets.  \begin{enumerate} \item If $f(A)\cup V(f)\subset B$, then every complex structure on $(\S^2, B)$ can be pulled back to a complex structure on $(\S^2, A)$, and this induces the map  $f^*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.  \item If $A\subset B$, then forgetting the points $B\backslash A$ induces the map $i_*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.   \end{enumerate} If $f(A)\cup V(f)\cup A\subset B,$ then the deformation space is defined by $$\D_f:=\{\tau\in \Teich(B): f^*(\tau)=i_*(\tau)\}.$$ Consider a quadratic rational map $f$ with critical points $c_1$ and $c_2$. Assume that  $c_1$ belongs to a cycle of length $4$, and the critical value $v=f(c_2)$ does not belong to the cycle. By taking  $$A=\{c_1, f(c_1), f^{\circ 2}(c_1), f^{\circ 3}(c_1)\}, \quad B=A\cup \{v\},$$ we get a deformation space $\D_f\subset \Teich(B)$. Its image in the moduli space is the set of conjugacy classes of quadratic rational maps with the properties described above.  Explicitly describe a simple closed curve $\gamma\subset (\S^2, B)$ such that a power of the Dehn twist around this curve preserves the deformation space, and its action on the set of connected components of $\D_f$ has an infinite orbit.

Let $f:\S^2\to \S^2$ be a branched cover, $V(f)$ be the set of its critical values,  and $A, B\subset \S^2$ be  finite sets.  \begin{enumerate} \item If $f(A)\cup V(f)\subset B$, then every complex structure on $(\S^2, B)$ can be pulled back to a complex structure on $(\S^2, A)$, and this induces the map  $f^*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.  \item If $A\subset B$, then forgetting the points $B\backslash A$ induces the map $i_*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.   \end{enumerate} If $f(A)\cup V(f)\cup A\subset B,$ then the deformation space is defined by $$\D_f:=\{\tau\in \Teich(B): f^*(\tau)=i_*(\tau)\}.$$ Consider a quadratic rational map $f$ with critical points $c_1$ and $c_2$. Assume that  $c_1$ belongs to a cycle of length $4$, and the critical value $v=f(c_2)$ does not belong to the cycle. By taking  $$A=\{c_1, f(c_1), f^{\circ 2}(c_1), f^{\circ 3}(c_1)\}, \quad B=A\cup \{v\},$$ we get a deformation space $\D_f\subset \Teich(B)$. Its image in the moduli space is the set of conjugacy classes of quadratic rational maps with the properties described above.  Explicitly describe a simple closed curve $\gamma\subset (\S^2, B)$ such that a power of the Dehn twist around this curve preserves the deformation space, and its action on the set of connected components of $\D_f$ has an infinite orbit.

Its image in the moduli space is the set of conjugacy classes of quadratic rational maps with the properties described above. ## Notation and background (shared context; claims marked "heuristic" are NOT verified)

Write the 4-cycle as a_0 = c_1, a_1 = f(c_1), a_2, a_3 (with f(a_3) = a_0), so A = {a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3}, B = A ∪ {v}, the critical values are a_1 and v, and Teich(B) has complex dimension 2, Teich(A) dimension 1, D_f dimension 1 (by Epstein transversality D_f is a smooth 1-dimensional complex submanifold).

Framework (standard, but you must justify anything you use):
* PMod(S^2,B) acts on Teich(B) by changing the marking. If φ ∈ PMod(S^2,B) has a lift φ~ (f∘φ~ = φ∘f) fixing A pointwise, then f^*(φ·τ) = φ~·f^*(τ), and i_*(φ·τ) = i(φ)·i_*(τ), where i : PMod(S^2,B) → PMod(S^2,A) forgets v. Hence if φ~ = i(φ) in PMod(S^2,A), then φ preserves D_f. Let G be the group of such φ (the "liftable-and-compatible" subgroup).
* Let W be the image of D_f in moduli space M_{0,5} = Teich(B)/PMod(S^2,B) (the curve of conjugacy classes of quadratic maps with a marked critical 4-cycle and marked other critical value v, v not in the cycle). If τ_1, τ_2 ∈ D_f lie over the same point of W then τ_2 = φ·τ_1 with φ ∈ G. So G acts transitively on fibers of D_f → W; if D_0 is a component and G_0 ⊂ G its stabilizer, then (when W is connected) π_0(D_f) ≅ G/G_0, and the ⟨φ⟩-orbit of D_0 is infinite iff no nonzero power of φ lies in G_0.
* PMod(S^2,B) is torsion free and acts freely, so D_0 → W is a covering and G_0 is the image of π_1(W) → π_1(M_{0,5}) = PMod(S^2,B) (monodromy of the inclusion W ⊂ M_{0,5}), up to conjugacy depending on base points.

Lifting computations (heuristic, check them):
* If γ surrounds v and a_j with j ∈ {0,2,3} (one critical value inside), then f^{-1}(γ) is a single curve δ mapping with degree 2, bounding a disk containing c_2, a_{j-1} and the other preimage a'_{j-1} of a_j, so rel A, δ is peripheral; also i(γ) is peripheral. Then T_γ^2 lifts to T_δ, which is trivial in PMod(S^2,A), so T_γ^2 ∈ G.
* BUT: W has punctures where f(c_2) = a_j (c_2 strictly preperiodic onto the cycle). A small loop in W around such a puncture has monodromy T_γ^m for a curve γ around {v,a_j} (the "short" one in that degenerating configuration, transported to the base point), m = local order of contact. So for those particular curves a power of T_γ lies in G_0 and the orbit is FINITE. So the answer curve cannot be one of those; it must be either a curve around {v,a_j} drawn along a "different" arc, or a curve around two cycle points, or around {v,a_1} (both critical values: f^{-1}(γ) is then two curves each mapping with degree 1, bounding an annulus containing c_1, c_2).

If the image of H_1(W) in H_1(M_{0,5}) ⊗ Q does not contain the class of T_γ, no power of T_γ lies in G_0. (Whether W has genus 0, its punctures, and where it meets the boundary divisors of M̄_{0,5} must then be computed.) ledger and the index first, then the previous round's result files — each file once, in full.

whose status is no answer; a partial query's .partial.md is screened by the same test as a finished file —
being unfinished is not itself degenerate), and ignore every file you marked DEGENERATE in everything below.

You are directing a structured multi-round attempt at a hard mathematics problem. Each round, you compose
queries that are sent independently to a deep reasoning engine with a very large thinking budget; the
results come back as files, and you fold what they established into a running summary before composing the
next round. This is round 1 of at most 14. You may conclude in this round, before round 4,
as soon as the claims ledger holds the headline goal settled — a PROVED or REFUTED line tagged [GOAL] ("PROVED:
[GOAL] …") — and at least two PROVED lines tagged [AUDIT]. Each [AUDIT] line is the certification returned by a
separate verify query that checked the complete written proof chain (not a sketch or outline); it must name
that query's locator (e.g. round3_q2) and cite the [GOAL] line, or a line it cites, by ledger id written "entry
12" or "#12" — at least one [AUDIT] line citing the [GOAL] line itself. When the ledger qualifies, decide in
this step between two things: conclude, or raise the goal (item 2 below says when and how) and compose a wave
for the raised goal. Do not run further waves merely to reach round 4 or to polish — the
proof-writing steps that follow do the polishing. Tag lines as they arise. If the ledger does not yet qualify,
compose a wave (the audit rule below says when it must contain verify queries).

previous summary and is the only memory later rounds (and the final proof assembly) have of what came
before, so carry forward everything still relevant. Record: what has been established, citing the result
file that showed it (e.g. round2_q3); promising partial progress; dead ends, and why each is dead; and the
open gaps that stand between the current state and the goal. Be honest — an overclaimed summary poisons
every later round. Keep it under 6000 words. Then decide where to target next: end the summary with a
section naming where the next round should concentrate — sharpening the strongest partial result, closing
the most load-bearing open gap, verifying something the attempt now depends on, or abandoning a dead line for
a fresh lens. Early rounds usually explore (varied independent reformulations and approaches); later rounds
usually exploit (focused attempts, verification of key steps). The choice is yours each round.

line recording that a separate verify query checked a complete written proof chain (name that query's
locator and cite the entry it certifies as "entry N" or "#N"). Tag lines as they arise. In round 1 write
exactly one [GOAL] line. If the problem fixes the claim to be settled, that claim — the whole claim as posed,
all parts — is the goal; if the task is
open-ended (improve, extend or strengthen a given work; find a significant result about something), choose
the goal now — one precise statement, the most significant result you judge this attempt can establish — and
record it as the [GOAL] line, OPEN until settled. (i) Status lines. Write a further [GOAL] line for the same
claim only when its status changes (OPEN → PROVED or REFUTED, or back to OPEN when a verify query finds a

already numbered when their answers return — or to come back to it under (iv) below; never merely to re-word

one) if it turned out false, ill-posed or already known, and also if you find it is narrower than, or
different from, the claim the problem itself poses — then the posed claim is the new goal (a replacement, not

stronger statement, or the general case of what was proved — write the new statement as an OPEN [GOAL] line

below, which direct a wave at a stalled statement only while it stays the goal: a step that comes back
composes no queries other than any verify queries the audit rule still requires for the goal it returns to (one audit wave, then
conclude). Other than coming back to a goal already proved, do not swap a goal for a weaker one because it is
proving hard: what was established toward an unreached goal is presented by the proof-writing steps as it
stands. Stronger or further results that you do not adopt as the goal stay as ordinary PROVED/OPEN lines and belong in the proof's "Other routes" section. (iv) Coming back. To come back to
a goal proved earlier (the raised statement did not yield), re-state it in this round's block as a "PROVED:

form (count it: if /data/output/logs/prob-007/work/math-proof-run/ledger.md ends at entry 23 and the re-stated goal is the second line of your block, it

no queries (if you raise the goal in this step, compose a wave for it instead — never write

(consecutive numbers) aimed at the target you chose. While the [GOAL] line is OPEN, parallel queries are

target, not rewordings of one attempt. Once a complete written proof (or refutation) of the [GOAL] claim is in

at what the final proof document will need (a corollary's full write-up, the proof of a lemma that was only
cited, an independent second proof). If instead you raise the goal in this step (item 2), the wave does not
shrink: the verify queries for the proved chain still go out — when their certifications return in a later
round, record them as [AUDIT] lines naming their locators and citing by number the PROVED entry of the goal
they certify, even though the goal has since moved on — and the rest of the wave, up to the cap, is composed
for the new OPEN [GOAL] line. When this brief carries the escalation rule below, that part of the wave follows
it, with the raised statement as the [GOAL] claim of which no proof is in hand: first go back and give the
summary its 'The chain and the missing statement' section for the raised statement (summary rule (iii); if
nothing yet reduces it, the raised statement itself is the missing statement, and its OPEN [GOAL] line serves
as its ledger entry), then compose that part of the wave under the escalation rule. Each query must be
self-contained: the reasoning engine sees ONLY that query file followed by the complete problem statement — no
summary, no ledger, no other results, no other round — so include, inline, any prior result or partial
argument the query builds on (splice long passages in from the answer file with the shell rather than
retyping them). Do NOT copy the problem statement itself into any query.
Targeting rule (applies every round). Of the queries you compose, at least half (rounded up) must ATTEMPT
open questions this run has itself flagged: the open questions named in result files, the OPEN claims in
the ledger, and the open gaps in your summary. Mark each such query by making its FIRST line exactly
"kind: attempt", and name inside it the specific open question it attempts. An attempt query tries to SETTLE
its question — prove it, refute it, or reduce it to something strictly easier — not to survey it, re-derive
known ground around it, or polish the document. A verdict that a question is "established: open" (or that
the goal is beyond the state of the art) is NOT final and must not be inherited by later rounds as settled:
reopen it and aim attempt queries directly at it.
Audit rule (applies every round). Whenever a result file in hand gives a complete written proof (or
refutation) of the [GOAL] claim — or of a goal you raised away from, in this step or earlier (not the
refutation of a goal you raised to: item 2 (iii)) — that fewer
than two verify queries have yet certified, at least as many of this round's queries as are still missing (two, or one)
must be independent verify queries of that written chain — if several result files each give a complete proof,
pick the most complete one and send both verify queries against that same chain. Each carries the complete argument verbatim —
assemble the query file with the shell from the answer file (cat, sed; from the partial file, under the
exception given with the file list above), do not retype or paraphrase it — and
asks for a step-by-step check of every inference, ending in an explicit verdict on whether the chain proves
the claim exactly as stated; they count as attempt queries (first line "kind: attempt", naming the [GOAL]
entry they audit); two certifications satisfy the gate — add a third only if it checks something the two do
not. When such a certification comes back positive, record it as a PROVED [AUDIT] line naming its locator and
citing, by number, the [GOAL] entry it certifies (that goal's settled line, even if the goal has since been
raised); when the ledger then qualifies (see above), conclude.

choice, or in a decision to conclude — first read that result's answer file and work from what it actually
says, not from the summary's paraphrase of it.

change: raised — entry N, proved in DIR/roundK_qJ.answer.md (certified by M verify queries so far), is …; the
goal is now …").

Problem statement (for reference — /data/output/logs/prob-007/work/math-proof-run/problem.md is the authoritative text; go by the file wherever this copy differs or looks garbled):
Let $f:\S^2\to \S^2$ be a branched cover, $V(f)$ be the set of its critical values,  and $A, B\subset \S^2$ be  finite sets.  \begin{enumerate} \item If $f(A)\cup V(f)\subset B$, then every complex structure on $(\S^2, B)$ can be pulled back to a complex structure on $(\S^2, A)$, and this induces the map  $f^*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.  \item If $A\subset B$, then forgetting the points $B\backslash A$ induces the map $i_*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.   \end{enumerate} If $f(A)\cup V(f)\cup A\subset B,$ then the deformation space is defined by $$\D_f:=\{\tau\in \Teich(B): f^*(\tau)=i_*(\tau)\}.$$ Consider a quadratic rational map $f$ with critical points $c_1$ and $c_2$. Assume that  $c_1$ belongs to a cycle of length $4$, and the critical value $v=f(c_2)$ does not belong to the cycle. By taking  $$A=\{c_1, f(c_1), f^{\circ 2}(c_1), f^{\circ 3}(c_1)\}, \quad B=A\cup \{v\},$$ we get a deformation space $\D_f\subset \Teich(B)$. Its image in the moduli space is the set of conjugacy classes of quadratic rational maps with the properties described above.  Explicitly describe a simple closed curve $\gamma\subset (\S^2, B)$ such that a power of the Dehn twist around this curve preserves the deformation space, and its action on the set of connected components of $\D_f$ has an infinite orbit.

I haven't concluded; this is round 1 and there are no earlier results. I wrote 4 query files, and all 4 are attempt queries aimed at the [GOAL].

**Target:** find an explicit curve γ and a power k so that T_γ^k preserves D_f, then prove that no nonzero power of T_γ^k fixes a component of D_f.

Each query attacks this from a different side:
- **q1:** a full attempt, using a homology (abelianization) obstruction.
- **q2:** an explicit computation of Per_4(0), its image curve W in M_{0,5}, W's punctures, and the image of H_1(W).
- **q3:** working out how curves pull back under a concrete model map, to find which twist powers preserve D_f.
- **q4:** proofs of the structural facts, the local picture of the forgetful map on D_f, and a test for when the orbit is infinite.

All four queries share a background block, and its claims are marked as unverified. One of them warns that, by my unchecked argument, a curve drawn around v and one cycle point along the short arc probably gives a finite orbit.

The ledger block has one line: the OPEN [GOAL].

- round1_q2.md
- round1_q3.md
- round1_q4.md

# round1_q1: partial answer (the main claim is not proved)

Notation: a_0=c_1, a_{i+1}=f(a_i), a_4=a_0. The critical values are a_1 and v. G is the group of φ in PMod(S^2,B) that have a lift φ~ with φ~ = i(φ) in PMod(S^2,A). Elements of G preserve D_f. This follows from the task's framework: f^*(φτ)=φ~ f^*(τ) and i_*(φτ)=i(φ) i_*(τ).

## Lemma 1 (proved). Curves around v and a_j, j in {0,2,3}, give twist-squares in G.
Setup: γ bounds a disk D with D∩B={v,a_j}.
- D contains exactly one critical value, v. So f^{-1}(D) is a single disk D~, mapping 2:1 and branched at c_2. Its boundary δ=f^{-1}(γ) maps to γ with degree 2.
- B∩D~ consists of the preimages of a_j and v. These are a_{j-1} (in A), another point a'_{j-1} (not in A), and the preimages of v (not in A).
- Since j≠1, a_{j-1}≠a_0... except in the case j=1, which is excluded. In every allowed case D~ contains exactly one point of A, so δ is peripheral in (S^2,A).
- T_γ^2 lifts to T_δ, because the degree-2 cover unwinds a double twist into a single twist. T_δ is trivial in PMod(S^2,A).
- i(T_γ)=1 as well, since γ encloses only one point of A.
- Therefore T_γ^2 ∈ G, and T_γ^2 preserves D_f.

## Lemma 2 (proved). Curves around the two critical values are not in G.
Setup: γ bounds a disk D with D∩B={a_1,v}.
- f^{-1}(D) is an annulus containing c_1=a_0 and c_2. It is bounded by curves δ_1 and δ_2, each mapping with degree 1.
- The two complementary disks split {a_1,a_2,a_3}. Each power T_γ^k lifts to T_{δ_1}^k T_{δ_2}^k, while i(T_γ)=1.
- If the split is 2/1, one δ_i is essential rel A. Then no nonzero power of T_γ lies in G.
- So this kind of curve is a candidate only when the split is 3/0, and in that case the twist acts trivially rel A.

## Proposed answer (claimed, not proved)
Take γ to be the boundary of a regular neighbourhood of an arc α from v to a_j, with j ∈ {0,2,3}. Choose α so that γ is **not** the curve that pinches at the puncture of W (the image of D_f in M_{0,5}) where f(c_2) collides with a_j. Concretely, α is obtained from the "pinching" arc α_0 by sliding its endpoint once around a second cycle point.

By Lemma 1, the power T_γ^2 preserves D_f.

The expected reason for an infinite orbit is the abelianization obstruction:
- The class of T_γ in H_1(M_{0,5}) = Z^5 equals the class of the twist about any curve surrounding {v,a_j}.
- So the obstruction has to come from a non-abelian quotient, or from the cusp argument. A parabolic element of G_0 acting on the disk D_0 must be conjugate within G_0 to a cusp monodromy of W. W has one cusp per collision type (v=a_j for each j, plus the degenerations of the cycle).
- If T_γ^{2n} were in G_0, then γ would be G_0-conjugate to a pinching curve α_0-type. Excluding this requires the explicit combinatorics of W.

I recall, without having checked it, that this is the mechanism in Hironaka–Koch, "A disconnected deformation space of rational maps". There, a twist of this kind has an infinite orbit on π_0(D_f).

## Open
- The proof that ⟨T_γ^2⟩ has an infinite orbit on π_0(D_f) is not given.
- Neither are the explicit computation of W (its genus, cusps and cusp monodromies) and the exclusion of γ from the G_0-conjugates of the cusp curves.

Notation: a_0=c_1, a_1=f(a_0), a_2, a_3, with f(a_3)=a_0. Normalize so that a_0=0, a_1=∞, a_2=1, a_3=t.
- 0 is critical and f(0)=∞, so f(z)=(αz²+βz+γ)/z². From f(∞)=1 we get α=1, so f(z)=1+β/z+γ/z².
- f(1)=t gives t=1+β+γ. f(t)=0 gives t²+βt+γ=0.
- Solving: β=(t²+t−1)/(1−t) and γ=t(1−2t)/(1−t).

So Per_4(0) with a marked cycle is rational, with parameter t.
- Other critical point: c_2=−2γ/β = −2t(1−2t)/(t²+t−1).
- Other critical value: v = 1−β²/(4γ). Write D=4t(1−2t)(1−t). Then:
  - v = −(t²−3t+1)²/D,
  - v−1 = −(t²+t−1)²/D,
  - v−t = −(3t²−3t+1)²/D.
  These follow from the identities (t²+t−1)²−D=(t²−3t+1)² and D(1−t)−(t²+t−1)²=−(3t²−3t+1)². I checked both by expansion.

## (b) Punctures of W
Fixing (a_0,a_1,a_2)=(0,∞,1) uses up the Möbius freedom, so t determines the marked conjugacy class. This gives the map W → M_{0,5}, t ↦ (0,∞,1,t,v(t)). W is the t-line minus 10 points:
- t = 0, 1, ∞, 1/2: degenerations. Either cycle points collide or the degree drops.
- The 2 roots of t²+t−1: here v=1=a_2, with contact order 2.
- The 2 roots of t²−3t+1: here v=0=a_0, with contact order 2.
- The 2 roots of 3t²−3t+1: here v=t=a_3, with contact order 2.

v never equals ∞=a_1 except at degenerate points.

## (c) Abelianization (proved)
In H_1(M_{0,5}) ≅ Z^5, use the coordinates given by the winding numbers of the functions t, t−1, v, v−1, v−t. These correspond to the classes e_{a3a0}, e_{a3a2}, e_{va0}, e_{va2}, e_{va3}. The class of a loop around a puncture p is the vector of orders of these five functions at p:
- t=0: (1,0,−1,−1,−1)
- t=1: (0,1,−1,−1,−1)
- t=1/2: (0,0,−1,−1,−1)
- t=∞: (−1,−1,−1,−1,−1)
- each root of t²−3t+1: (0,0,2,0,0)
- each root of t²+t−1: (0,0,0,2,0)
- each root of 3t²−3t+1: (0,0,0,0,2)

These vectors span a sublattice of rank 5. So the image of H_1(W) in H_1(M_{0,5}) has full rank (finite index; its index divides 2^3). **Conclusion: the abelian obstruction is insufficient.** For every curve γ, some power of the class of T_γ lies in the image of H_1(W). A finer, non-abelian invariant is needed.

## (d) Candidate curve and status
**Candidate (not proved):** γ is the curve surrounding the two critical values a_1=f(c_1) and v, and separating them from {a_0,a_2,a_3}.

Lifting structure (proved):
- f^{-1}(disk bounded by γ) is an annulus containing c_1=a_0 and c_2. This is a degree-2 cover of a disk branched over two points.
- The complement of that annulus is two disks. Each maps homeomorphically onto the outside of γ.
- So f^{-1}(γ)=δ_1⊔δ_2, each component mapping with degree 1, and T_γ lifts to T_{δ_1}T_{δ_2}.

For T_γ^k to lie in G, we need the lift to equal i(T_γ^k)=T_{i(γ)}^k in PMod(S²,A), where i(γ) surrounds {a_1}∪... rel A. Note that i(γ) is peripheral rel A. So this requires each δ_j to be peripheral rel A, or to be isotopic to each other with cancelling twists. I have not verified which case occurs for this map. This is the remaining step that is needed.

I recall that the problem appears in Hironaka–Koch, "A disconnected deformation space of rational maps". I am citing this from memory and have not checked which curve they use.

**Open:**
1. Verify that a power of T_γ lies in G.
2. Prove that no power of it lies in G_0 = image of π_1(W) (a free group of rank 9). One possible route is a non-abelian quotient, e.g. the action on curves/arcs or a finite-index congruence quotient. Another is the parabolic argument: a twist power in G_0 must be conjugate to a puncture loop of W, and the puncture loops have monodromy twists about curves around {v,a_j} for j=0,2,3, or about curves from degenerations of the cycle.

I have **not** proved an infinite orbit for any explicit γ.

=== END OF ANSWER round1_q2 ===

=== round1_q1.answer
# round1_q1: partial answer (the main claim is not proved)

Notation: a_0=c_1, a_{i+1}=f(a_i), a_4=a_0. The critical values are a_1 and v. G is the group of φ in PMod(S^2,B) that have a lift φ~ with φ~ = i(φ) in PMod(S^2,A). Elements of G preserve D_f. This follows from the task's framework: f^*(φτ)=φ~ f^*(τ) and i_*(φτ)=i(φ) i_*(τ).

## Lemma 1 (proved). Curves around v and a_j, j in {0,2,3}, give twist-squares in G.
Setup: γ bounds a disk D with D∩B={v,a_j}.
- D contains exactly one critical value, v. So f^{-1}(D) is a single disk D~, mapping 2:1 and branched at c_2. Its boundary δ=f^{-1}(γ) maps to γ with degree 2.
- B∩D~ consists of the preimages of a_j and v. These are a_{j-1} (in A), another point a'_{j-1} (not in A), and the preimages of v (not in A).
- Since j≠1, a_{j-1}≠a_0... except in the case j=1, which is excluded. In every allowed case D~ contains exactly one point of A, so δ is peripheral in (S^2,A).
- T_γ^2 lifts to T_δ, because the degree-2 cover unwinds a double twist into a single twist. T_δ is trivial in PMod(S^2,A).
- i(T_γ)=1 as well, since γ encloses only one point of A.
- Therefore T_γ^2 ∈ G, and T_γ^2 preserves D_f.

## Lemma 2 (proved). Curves around the two critical values are not in G.
Setup: γ bounds a disk D with D∩B={a_1,v}.
- f^{-1}(D) is an annulus containing c_1=a_0 and c_2. It is bounded by curves δ_1 and δ_2, each mapping with degree 1.
- The two complementary disks split {a_1,a_2,a_3}. Each power T_γ^k lifts to T_{δ_1}^k T_{δ_2}^k, while i(T_γ)=1.
- If the split is 2/1, one δ_i is essential rel A. Then no nonzero power of T_γ lies in G.
- So this kind of curve is a candidate only when the split is 3/0, and in that case the twist acts trivially rel A.

## Proposed answer (claimed, not proved)
Take γ to be the boundary of a regular neighbourhood of an arc α from v to a_j, with j ∈ {0,2,3}. Choose α so that γ is **not** the curve that pinches at the puncture of W (the image of D_f in M_{0,5}) where f(c_2) collides with a_j. Concretely, α is obtained from the "pinching" arc α_0 by sliding its endpoint once around a second cycle point.

By Lemma 1, the power T_γ^2 preserves D_f.

The expected reason for an infinite orbit is the abelianization obstruction:
- The class of T_γ in H_1(M_{0,5}) = Z^5 equals the class of the twist about any curve surrounding {v,a_j}.
- So the obstruction has to come from a non-abelian quotient, or from the cusp argument. A parabolic element of G_0 acting on the disk D_0 must be conjugate within G_0 to a cusp monodromy of W. W has one cusp per collision type (v=a_j for each j, plus the degenerations of the cycle).
- If T_γ^{2n} were in G_0, then γ would be G_0-conjugate to a pinching curve α_0-type. Excluding this requires the explicit combinatorics of W.

I recall, without having checked it, that this is the mechanism in Hironaka–Koch, "A disconnected deformation space of rational maps". There, a twist of this kind has an infinite orbit on π_0(D_f).

## Open
- The proof that ⟨T_γ^2⟩ has an infinite orbit on π_0(D_f) is not given.
- Neither are the explicit computation of W (its genus, cusps and cusp monodromies) and the exclusion of γ from the G_0-conjugates of the cusp curves.

=== END OF ANSWER round1_q1 ===
=== round1_q2.answer
# round1_q2 — explicit model of W and the abelian obstruction

## (a) Normal form and parametrization (proved by direct computation)
Notation: a_0=c_1, a_1=f(a_0), a_2, a_3, with f(a_3)=a_0. Normalize so that a_0=0, a_1=∞, a_2=1, a_3=t.
- 0 is critical and f(0)=∞, so f(z)=(αz²+βz+γ)/z². From f(∞)=1 we get α=1, so f(z)=1+β/z+γ/z².
- f(1)=t gives t=1+β+γ. f(t)=0 gives t²+βt+γ=0.
- Solving: β=(t²+t−1)/(1−t) and γ=t(1−2t)/(1−t).

So Per_4(0) with a marked cycle is rational, with parameter t.
- Other critical point: c_2=−2γ/β = −2t(1−2t)/(t²+t−1).
- Other critical value: v = 1−β²/(4γ). Write D=4t(1−2t)(1−t). Then:
  - v = −(t²−3t+1)²/D,
  - v−1 = −(t²+t−1)²/D,
  - v−t = −(3t²−3t+1)²/D.
  These follow from the identities (t²+t−1)²−D=(t²−3t+1)² and D(1−t)−(t²+t−1)²=−(3t²−3t+1)². I checked both by expansion.

## (b) Punctures of W
Fixing (a_0,a_1,a_2)=(0,∞,1) uses up the Möbius freedom, so t determines the marked conjugacy class. This gives the map W → M_{0,5}, t ↦ (0,∞,1,t,v(t)). W is the t-line minus 10 points:
- t = 0, 1, ∞, 1/2: degenerations. Either cycle points collide or the degree drops.
- The 2 roots of t²+t−1: here v=1=a_2, with contact order 2.
- The 2 roots of t²−3t+1: here v=0=a_0, with contact order 2.
- The 2 roots of 3t²−3t+1: here v=t=a_3, with contact order 2.

v never equals ∞=a_1 except at degenerate points.

## (c) Abelianization (proved)
In H_1(M_{0,5}) ≅ Z^5, use the coordinates given by the winding numbers of the functions t, t−1, v, v−1, v−t. These correspond to the classes e_{a3a0}, e_{a3a2}, e_{va0}, e_{va2}, e_{va3}. The class of a loop around a puncture p is the vector of orders of these five functions at p:
- t=0: (1,0,−1,−1,−1)
- t=1: (0,1,−1,−1,−1)
- t=1/2: (0,0,−1,−1,−1)
- t=∞: (−1,−1,−1,−1,−1)
- each root of t²−3t+1: (0,0,2,0,0)
- each root of t²+t−1: (0,0,0,2,0)
- each root of 3t²−3t+1: (0,0,0,0,2)

These vectors span a sublattice of rank 5. So the image of H_1(W) in H_1(M_{0,5}) has full rank (finite index; its index divides 2^3). **Conclusion: the abelian obstruction is insufficient.** For every curve γ, some power of the class of T_γ lies in the image of H_1(W). A finer, non-abelian invariant is needed.

## (d) Candidate curve and status
**Candidate (not proved):** γ is the curve surrounding the two critical values a_1=f(c_1) and v, and separating them from {a_0,a_2,a_3}.

Lifting structure (proved):
- f^{-1}(disk bounded by γ) is an annulus containing c_1=a_0 and c_2. This is a degree-2 cover of a disk branched over two points.
- The complement of that annulus is two disks. Each maps homeomorphically onto the outside of γ.
- So f^{-1}(γ)=δ_1⊔δ_2, each component mapping with degree 1, and T_γ lifts to T_{δ_1}T_{δ_2}.

For T_γ^k to lie in G, we need the lift to equal i(T_γ^k)=T_{i(γ)}^k in PMod(S²,A), where i(γ) surrounds {a_1}∪... rel A. Note that i(γ) is peripheral rel A. So this requires each δ_j to be peripheral rel A, or to be isotopic to each other with cancelling twists. I have not verified which case occurs for this map. This is the remaining step that is needed.

I recall that the problem appears in Hironaka–Koch, "A disconnected deformation space of rational maps". I am citing this from memory and have not checked which curve they use.

**Open:**
1. Verify that a power of T_γ lies in G.
2. Prove that no power of it lies in G_0 = image of π_1(W) (a free group of rank 9). One possible route is a non-abelian quotient, e.g. the action on curves/arcs or a finite-index congruence quotient. Another is the parabolic argument: a twist power in G_0 must be conjugate to a puncture loop of W, and the puncture loops have monodromy twists about curves around {v,a_j} for j=0,2,3, or about curves from degenerations of the cycle.

I have **not** proved an infinite orbit for any explicit γ.

=== END OF ANSWER round1_q2 ===
=== round1_q3.answer
# round1_q3: candidate curve and lifting computation (partial)

Notation: a_0=c_1, a_{k+1}=f(a_k), indices mod 4; A={a_0,..,a_3}, B=A∪{v}. The critical values are a_1 and v.

## Proposal (curve γ)
γ is the boundary of a small regular neighbourhood of an arc α in S^2∖(A) joining the two critical values a_1 and v. So γ surrounds exactly {a_1, v}, and α is chosen as described in Lemma 2 below.

## Lemma 1 (preimage of γ). Proved.
Let D be the disk bounded by γ containing a_1 and v, and D' the complementary disk, which contains a_0, a_2, a_3. D contains both critical values. By Riemann–Hurwitz, f^{-1}(D) is connected with Euler characteristic 2·1−2=0, so it is an annulus containing c_1=a_0 and c_2. D' contains no critical value, so f^{-1}(D') is two disks E_1, E_2, each mapped homeomorphically onto D'. Hence f^{-1}(γ)=δ_1⊔δ_2 with δ_i=∂E_i, and each δ_i maps to γ with degree 1. The points of A that lie in f^{-1}(D') are a_3, a_1, a_2 (the preimages in the cycle of a_0, a_2, a_3). Each E_i contains exactly one preimage of each of a_0, a_2, a_3. a_0 lies in the annulus.

## Lemma 2 (lifting criterion). Proved, standard.
Let φ∈PMod(S^2,B). Suppose φ has a lift φ~ with f∘φ~=φ∘f, φ~ fixing A pointwise, and φ~ = i(φ) in PMod(S^2,A). Then φ preserves D_f: if f^*τ=i_*τ, then f^*(φτ)=φ~·f^*τ=i(φ)·i_*τ=i_*(φτ).
Because each δ_i maps to γ with degree 1, T_γ lifts to T_{δ_1}T_{δ_2}. This lift fixes every point (it is supported in annular neighbourhoods of δ_1, δ_2, which avoid A). Rel A, i(γ) surrounds only a_1, so i(T_γ) is trivial in PMod(S^2,A). So T_γ∈G exactly when T_{δ_1}T_{δ_2} is trivial rel A. That happens iff each δ_i is peripheral rel A. Since a_0 lies in the annulus, this means: one disk, say E_1, contains all of a_1, a_2, a_3, and E_2 contains no point of A (it holds only the other preimages a_1', a_2', a_3'). **Choice of α:** choose the arc α (its isotopy class rel B) so that this splitting holds. Such a choice exists: changing α by a twist about a curve around {a_1, v} plus one more point moves the preimages of single points between E_1 and E_2. Under this choice, T_γ (power k=1; k=2 in any case suffices if a sign ambiguity arises) preserves D_f.
I have only sketched the existence of such an α. It is not fully verified.

## Infinite orbit. Heuristic, not proved.
Theorem (recalled, not proved here): π_0(D_f)≅G/G_0, where G_0 is the image of the monodromy π_1(W)→PMod(S^2,B). So the orbit of a component is infinite iff no power T_γ^n (n≠0) lies in G_0. A parabolic element of G_0 must come from a puncture of W at which γ is pinched. Here pinching γ means the critical values a_1 and v collide while a_0, a_2, a_3 stay apart. That is f(c_2)=f(c_1), which for a quadratic map forces c_1=c_2, so it cannot happen for any genuine map. The argument is then that no such cusp of W exists, which would make the orbit infinite. This step is incomplete: degenerations to the boundary of rational-map space have not been ruled out. The punctures where v=a_j, j≠1, give the curves around {v,a_j} instead. Those have finite orbits and are excluded on purpose.

I recall (from memory, unverified) that this example appears in Hironaka–Koch, "A disconnected deformation space of rational maps". I think they use a twist about a curve that separates the two critical values from the rest, but I could not confirm the exact curve.

## Status
- Proved: Lemma 1, the lifting criterion, and that T_γ∈G given the splitting condition on α.
- Sketched: existence of an arc α that gives that splitting.
- Open: a rigorous proof that the orbit on π_0(D_f) is infinite.

=== END OF ANSWER round1_q3 ===
=== round1_q4.answer
# round1_q4 answer

Notation: a_0=c_1, a_1=f(c_1), a_2, a_3 is the critical 4-cycle, A={a_0,...,a_3}, B=A∪{v}. The critical values are a_1 and v.

## The curve
Let γ be a simple closed curve in S^2∖B that bounds a disk Δ with Δ∩B={a_1,v}, so γ surrounds both critical values. In addition we need the outer disk Δ'=S^2∖Δ, which contains a_0,a_2,a_3, to have preimage under f consisting of two disks E_1,E_2, where E_1 contains a_1,a_2,a_3 and E_2 contains no point of A. The precise conditions are given in the Lemma.

## Lemma (T_γ preserves D_f). Proved.
Since Δ' contains no critical value, f^{-1}(Δ') is two disks E_1,E_2, each mapped homeomorphically onto Δ'. Then f^{-1}(Δ) is an annulus containing c_1,c_2, and f^{-1}(γ)=δ_1∪δ_2 with δ_i=∂E_i, each mapping with degree 1.

- The preimages of a_0,a_2,a_3 are {a_3,a_3'}, {a_1,a_1'}, {a_2,a_2'}. One of each pair lies in E_1 and the other in E_2.
- The point a_0=c_1 lies in the annulus.
- So the A-points outside the annulus are a_1,a_2,a_3. Choosing the arc that Δ thickens means choosing γ so that all three lie in the same disk E_1. This is always possible: pass from one choice to another by pushing v around loops, which permutes which sheet each preimage lies in.

With this choice, δ_2 bounds a disk with no point of A, and δ_1 bounds a disk whose complement contains only a_0. So both are peripheral in (S^2,A). The lift of T_γ is T_{δ_1}T_{δ_2}, which is trivial in PMod(S^2,A). Also i(T_γ) is trivial, because i(γ) encloses only a_1. Hence f^*(T_γ τ)=f^*(τ) and i_*(T_γ τ)=i_*(τ), so T_γ maps D_f to D_f. Here the power is k=1.

The 3/0 split is not automatic. With a 2/1 split, δ_1 is essential and T_γ^n is never in G for n≠0. So the arc choice is part of the answer.

## Infinite orbit: not proved here
The claim is that no nonzero power of T_γ stabilises a component D_0 of D_f, i.e. T_γ^n ∉ G_0 for n≠0. Then the T_γ-orbit of D_0 in π_0(D_f) is infinite. From memory, this is the theorem of Hironaka–Koch ("A disconnected deformation space of rational maps"). They use exactly a twist about a curve surrounding the two critical values, and show D_f has infinitely many components. I have not reproduced their argument.

The route I would take: compare the image of H_1(W) in H_1(M_{0,5}) with the class e_{a_1 v}. The cusps of W are where v collides with a_j, j=0,2,3, and their monodromies are powers of twists around {v,a_j}. One would need to show the class e_{a_1 v} is not in the span of the cusp classes and the other contributions from H_1(W). Steps not done: proving W is connected, and computing the full image of H_1(W).

Status:
- Proved: T_γ ∈ G for the explicit curve with the 3/0 lift condition.
- Cited, not proved: the infinite orbit.
- Open: a self-contained proof that T_γ^n ∉ G_0 for all n≠0.

=== END OF ANSWER round1_q4 ===

Open question attempted: the headline goal itself — produce an explicit simple closed curve γ in (S^2,B) and an integer k ≥ 1 such that T_γ^k preserves D_f and ⟨T_γ^k⟩ has an infinite orbit on π_0(D_f), with a complete proof.

Task. Settle the problem completely. Give (1) an explicit description of γ (which marked points it separates, and, since that alone does not determine a curve, precisely how it is drawn relative to the dynamics — e.g. relative to a concrete model map in the family, invariant arcs/real line, or the Hubbard-tree-like combinatorics of the 4-cycle), (2) a proof that some power T_γ^k preserves D_f (via the lifting criterion below or otherwise), and (3) a proof that no nonzero power of T_γ^k stabilizes a component of D_f, so the orbit of components is infinite. Be careful to make every step rigorous; where you use a structural fact (e.g. π_0(D_f) ≅ G/G_0, or G_0 = image of π_1(W)), prove it or give a precise reference-free argument. Let $f:\S^2\to \S^2$ be a branched cover, $V(f)$ be the set of its critical values,  and $A, B\subset \S^2$ be  finite sets.  \begin{enumerate} \item If $f(A)\cup V(f)\subset B$, then every complex structure on $(\S^2, B)$ can be pulled back to a complex structure on $(\S^2, A)$, and this induces the map  $f^*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.  \item If $A\subset B$, then forgetting the points $B\backslash A$ induces the map $i_*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.   \end{enumerate} If $f(A)\cup V(f)\cup A\subset B,$ then the deformation space is defined by $$\D_f:=\{\tau\in \Teich(B): f^*(\tau)=i_*(\tau)\}.$$ Consider a quadratic rational map $f$ with critical points $c_1$ and $c_2$. Assume that  $c_1$ belongs to a cycle of length $4$, and the critical value $v=f(c_2)$ does not belong to the cycle. By taking  $$A=\{c_1, f(c_1), f^{\circ 2}(c_1), f^{\circ 3}(c_1)\}, \quad B=A\cup \{v\},$$ we get a deformation space $\D_f\subset \Teich(B)$. Its image in the moduli space is the set of conjugacy classes of quadratic rational maps with the properties described above.  Explicitly describe a simple closed curve $\gamma\subset (\S^2, B)$ such that a power of the Dehn twist around this curve preserves the deformation space, and its action on the set of connected components of $\D_f$ has an infinite orbit.

# round2_q3 — answer (partial; main question remains OPEN)

## Plan
Decide (a)-(c) for the {v,a_j} family by using the quotient F̄ = F/<<ℓ_1>>. Result: this quotient gives NO obstruction (dead end, proved modulo one surjectivity lemma that is only sketched). The answer therefore probably has to come from the {a_1,v} family.

## 1. The forgetful map W → M_{0,4}(a_0,a_2,a_3,v) (PROVED by computation)
Send (0,1,t) to (0,1,∞) using m(z) = z(1−t)/(z−t), so m(0)=0, m(1)=1, m(t)=∞. With P=t²−3t+1, Q=t²+t−1, R=3t²−3t+1 and v=−P²/D, v−t=−R²/D (background item (2)):
  u(t) := m(v(t)) = (1−t)P²/R².
Check: (1−t)P² − R² = −t⁵−2t⁴+t³+2t²−t = −t(t²+t−1)² (expand P²=t⁴−6t³+11t²−6t+1, R²=9t⁴−18t³+15t²−6t+1). Hence
  u − 1 = −t Q²/R².
So u is a rational map of degree 5 with these fibres:
  u=0: t=1 (simple), roots of P (double);  u=1: t=0 (simple), roots of Q (double);  u=∞: t=∞ (simple, 5−4=1), roots of R (double).
Riemann–Hurwitz: 2·5−2 = 8, and these fibres account for 6, so there are 2 more simple critical points of u, outside these fibres. Also u(1/2) = (1/2)(1/16)/(1/16) = 1/2, which is not a puncture of the u-plane.

## 2. Consequence: the quotient F̄ gives no obstruction for the {v,a_j} curves (dead end)
The image of G_0 in PMod(S², {a_0,a_2,a_3,v}) ≅ π_1(C∖{0,1}) (≅ F̄, the point-push group of v) is u_*(π_1 W). The image of K is u_*(N). Here N is normally generated by the loops around t=1/2 and around the six roots. Its image is generated as follows:
- the loop around t=1/2 maps to a null-homotopic loop, since u(1/2)=1/2 is not a puncture;
- the loops around the six roots map to conjugates of the squares of the loops around 0, 1 and ∞, i.e. of ℓ_0², ℓ_2², ℓ_3².

Sketched lemma: u_*(π_1 W) = π_1(C∖{0,1}). Reason: the simple preimages t=1, 0, ∞ are punctures of W. Their small loops map to conjugates of single generator loops around 0, 1, ∞. Because u is a connected branched cover, these conjugates should generate the whole group. I did not check this fully.

If the lemma holds, the image of K in F̄ is the full normal closure of ℓ_0², ℓ_2², ℓ_3². The quotient F̄/<<ℓ_0², ℓ_2², ℓ_3²>> with ℓ_0ℓ_2ℓ_3 = 1 is the Klein four-group, which is finite. Every conjugate of ℓ_j² dies in it. So the image of T_γ² in F̄ lies in the image of K for every curve γ around {v,a_j}, and this quotient cannot detect an infinite orbit. Deciding the {v,a_j} family needs finer information about K inside F itself. That question is open.

## 3. Candidate answer (CONJECTURAL)
Take γ to be a curve around the two critical values {a_1, v} with the "3/0 split" of background item (6). Then T_γ lifts to a twist that is trivial relative to A, so T_γ ∈ G. Concrete choice: γ = T_β²(γ0), where
- γ0 is the cusp curve at t=1/2 (background item (4));
- β is any curve around {v, a_0}, so T_β² ∈ G by item (5).

Then T_γ = T_β² T_{γ0} T_β^{−2}. It preserves D_f and fixes the component T_β²·D_0.

Claimed but NOT proved: some component (equivalently, after conjugating, D_0) has an infinite ⟨T_γ⟩-orbit. By background item (7) this is the statement that no nonzero power of T_γ lies in K. In the quotient Q ≅ Z/2*Z/2*Z/2 of background item (8), this reduces to showing that a specific parabolic conjugate of ℓ̄_1 is not in the subgroup generated by the G_0-orbit of x̄_{1/2}. That needs the action of G_0 on Q, which I have not computed.

## Status
- Proved: the formula for u(t) and its fibres/ramification (§1).
- Sketched (one unchecked surjectivity lemma): the quotient F̄ cannot settle the {v,a_j} family (§2).
- Open: an explicit γ with a proof of an infinite orbit. Specifically, (i) whether some curve around {v,a_j} has no power of T_γ² in K; (ii) whether a 3/0 curve around {a_1,v} such as T_β²(γ0) has an infinite orbit.

Let $f:\S^2\to \S^2$ be a branched cover, $V(f)$ be the set of its critical values,  and $A, B\subset \S^2$ be  finite sets.  \begin{enumerate} \item If $f(A)\cup V(f)\subset B$, then every complex structure on $(\S^2, B)$ can be pulled back to a complex structure on $(\S^2, A)$, and this induces the map  $f^*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.  \item If $A\subset B$, then forgetting the points $B\backslash A$ induces the map $i_*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.   \end{enumerate} If $f(A)\cup V(f)\cup A\subset B,$ then the deformation space is defined by $$\D_f:=\{\tau\in \Teich(B): f^*(\tau)=i_*(\tau)\}.$$ Consider a quadratic rational map $f$ with critical points $c_1$ and $c_2$. Assume that  $c_1$ belongs to a cycle of length $4$, and the critical value $v=f(c_2)$ does not belong to the cycle. By taking  $$A=\{c_1, f(c_1), f^{\circ 2}(c_1), f^{\circ 3}(c_1)\}, \quad B=A\cup \{v\},$$ we get a deformation space $\D_f\subset \Teich(B)$. Its image in the moduli space is the set of conjugacy classes of quadratic rational maps with the properties described above.  Explicitly describe a simple closed curve $\gamma\subset (\S^2, B)$ such that a power of the Dehn twist around this curve preserves the deformation space, and its action on the set of connected components of $\D_f$ has an infinite orbit.

content.content:
Let $f:\S^2\to \S^2$ be a branched cover, $V(f)$ be the set of its critical values,  and $A, B\subset \S^2$ be  finite sets.  \begin{enumerate} \item If $f(A)\cup V(f)\subset B$, then every complex structure on $(\S^2, B)$ can be pulled back to a complex structure on $(\S^2, A)$, and this induces the map  $f^*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.  \item If $A\subset B$, then forgetting the points $B\backslash A$ induces the map $i_*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.   \end{enumerate} If $f(A)\cup V(f)\cup A\subset B,$ then the deformation space is defined by $$\D_f:=\{\tau\in \Teich(B): f^*(\tau)=i_*(\tau)\}.$$ Consider a quadratic rational map $f$ with critical points $c_1$ and $c_2$. Assume that  $c_1$ belongs to a cycle of length $4$, and the critical value $v=f(c_2)$ does not belong to the cycle. By taking  $$A=\{c_1, f(c_1), f^{\circ 2}(c_1), f^{\circ 3}(c_1)\}, \quad B=A\cup \{v\},$$ we get a deformation space $\D_f\subset \Teich(B)$. Its image in the moduli space is the set of conjugacy classes of quadratic rational maps with the properties described above.  Explicitly describe a simple closed curve $\gamma\subset (\S^2, B)$ such that a power of the Dehn twist around this curve preserves the deformation space, and its action on the set of connected components of $\D_f$ has an infinite orbit. === Q1
# round2_q1 — partial answer (route via Q = Z/2*Z/2*Z/2 not completed)

## Candidate curve (conjectured, not proved here)
Use the normalization of item (2) with a real base parameter t in (0,1/2), so that 0 = a_0 < t = a_3 < 1/2 < 1 = a_2, a_1 = ∞, and v(t) real. Take γ to be the boundary of a thin neighborhood of an arc from v to a_1 = ∞ that, instead of following the real line (the arc whose twist is the cusp monodromy x_{1/2} = T_{γ0}, item (4)), first goes once around a_0 and a_3. Equivalently γ = h(γ0), where h = T_c^2 and c is the curve enclosing {a_0, a_3} along [0,t]. Since T_c^2 is the t = 0 cusp monodromy up to the v-correction, it lies in G, so by item (6) γ has the 3/0 split and T_γ = h T_{γ0} h^{-1} ∈ G (so k = 1 suffices). This gives (c) for this γ, modulo the item-(4) identification.

I recall from memory, without being able to check it, that Hironaka and Koch ("A disconnected deformation space of rational maps") treat exactly this example and show that D_f has infinitely many components, using a Dehn twist of this kind. I cannot reconstruct their curve precisely, so the description above is my own candidate and not a citation.

## What is proved here
- Items (1), (5), (6) as given: for any 3/0 curve γ around {a_1, v}, T_γ ∈ G, and the orbit of D_0 under ⟨T_γ⟩ is infinite if and only if T_γ^n ∉ K for every n ≠ 0 (item 7).
- Negative observation: for curves around {v, a_j} with j ∈ {0, 2, 3}, the quotients F/⟨⟨ℓ_1⟩⟩ and its mod-2 homology cannot separate T_γ^2 from K, because both are generated by conjugates of the squares ℓ_j^2. So that family needs a finer invariant.

## Open
(a)/(b) were not carried out. I did not compute x_{1/2} explicitly, the G_0-action on Q, or whether the image of K in Q avoids the parabolic image of T_γ^n. So the main claim — that T_γ^n ∉ K for every n ≠ 0 — remains OPEN in this file.

=== END OF ANSWER round2_q1 ===
=== Q2
# round2_q2 — partial answer

Status: the main goal is NOT settled. Below I separate what I checked from what is still open.

## Checked (short arguments)

A. Curves around {v, a_j}, j in {0,2,3} (item 5). Let Delta be a disk with Delta ∩ B = {v, a_j}. It contains exactly one critical value, v, so f^{-1}(Delta) is a single disk mapped 2:1. That disk meets A only in a_{j-1}, so its boundary is peripheral rel A. Hence T_gamma^2 lifts to a map that is trivial rel A. Also i(T_gamma) = 1. So T_gamma^2 ∈ G for every such curve. Explicit curve: for real t in (0, 1/2), the points are ordered on the real line. One can take gamma to be the boundary of a thin neighbourhood of the real segment joining v(t) to the nearest point of A, provided that segment contains no other marked point.

B. The quotient tests in item (8) cannot separate these curves.
- In F/<<l_1>> ≅ F_2, the image of K lies in the normal closure of {l_0^2, l_2^2, l_3^2}. The image of T_gamma^{2n} is a conjugate of l_j^{2n}, which also lies in that normal closure. So this quotient gives no obstruction.
- In Q = Z/2*Z/2*Z/2, the image of T_gamma^2 is trivial. So Q gives no obstruction either.

Any invariant that works must use the actual G_0-orbit structure of the generators of K, not only their normal closures.

C. A curve gamma around {a_1, v} with a 3/0 split has T_gamma ∈ G (item 6). In Q, its image is a parabolic conjugate of l_1. The image of K in Q is generated by G_0-translates of x_{1/2}. To show the orbit is infinite, one would need to show that the G_0-orbit of x_{1/2} in Q never generates a nonzero power of the parabolic element given by T_gamma. I did not complete this.

## Proposed answer (conjectural, not proved)

Take gamma to be a simple closed curve around {v, a_j} as in A, chosen not to be one of the six cusp curves of item (4) up to G_0-conjugacy. For example, take the curve around v and a_0 whose arc passes once around a_2. Take k = 2. Then T_gamma^2 preserves D_f (proved, part A). The claim that its orbit on pi_0(D_f) is infinite is NOT proved here.

## Open
- Compute the monodromy generators of G_0 explicitly (task part (a)).
- Build a non-abelian invariant that separates <T_gamma^2> from K.

=== END OF ANSWER round2_q2 ===
=== Q3
# round2_q3 — answer (partial; main question remains OPEN)

## Plan
Decide (a)-(c) for the {v,a_j} family by using the quotient F̄ = F/<<ℓ_1>>. Result: this quotient gives NO obstruction (dead end, proved modulo one surjectivity lemma that is only sketched). The answer therefore probably has to come from the {a_1,v} family.

## 1. The forgetful map W → M_{0,4}(a_0,a_2,a_3,v) (PROVED by computation)
Send (0,1,t) to (0,1,∞) using m(z) = z(1−t)/(z−t), so m(0)=0, m(1)=1, m(t)=∞. With P=t²−3t+1, Q=t²+t−1, R=3t²−3t+1 and v=−P²/D, v−t=−R²/D (background item (2)):
  u(t) := m(v(t)) = (1−t)P²/R².
Check: (1−t)P² − R² = −t⁵−2t⁴+t³+2t²−t = −t(t²+t−1)² (expand P²=t⁴−6t³+11t²−6t+1, R²=9t⁴−18t³+15t²−6t+1). Hence
  u − 1 = −t Q²/R².
So u is a rational map of degree 5 with these fibres:
  u=0: t=1 (simple), roots of P (double);  u=1: t=0 (simple), roots of Q (double);  u=∞: t=∞ (simple, 5−4=1), roots of R (double).
Riemann–Hurwitz: 2·5−2 = 8, and these fibres account for 6, so there are 2 more simple critical points of u, outside these fibres. Also u(1/2) = (1/2)(1/16)/(1/16) = 1/2, which is not a puncture of the u-plane.

## 2. Consequence: the quotient F̄ gives no obstruction for the {v,a_j} curves (dead end)
The image of G_0 in PMod(S², {a_0,a_2,a_3,v}) ≅ π_1(C∖{0,1}) (≅ F̄, the point-push group of v) is u_*(π_1 W). The image of K is u_*(N). Here N is normally generated by the loops around t=1/2 and around the six roots. Its image is generated as follows:
- the loop around t=1/2 maps to a null-homotopic loop, since u(1/2)=1/2 is not a puncture;
- the loops around the six roots map to conjugates of the squares of the loops around 0, 1 and ∞, i.e. of ℓ_0², ℓ_2², ℓ_3².

Sketched lemma: u_*(π_1 W) = π_1(C∖{0,1}). Reason: the simple preimages t=1, 0, ∞ are punctures of W. Their small loops map to conjugates of single generator loops around 0, 1, ∞. Because u is a connected branched cover, these conjugates should generate the whole group. I did not check this fully.

If the lemma holds, the image of K in F̄ is the full normal closure of ℓ_0², ℓ_2², ℓ_3². The quotient F̄/<<ℓ_0², ℓ_2², ℓ_3²>> with ℓ_0ℓ_2ℓ_3 = 1 is the Klein four-group, which is finite. Every conjugate of ℓ_j² dies in it. So the image of T_γ² in F̄ lies in the image of K for every curve γ around {v,a_j}, and this quotient cannot detect an infinite orbit. Deciding the {v,a_j} family needs finer information about K inside F itself. That question is open.

## 3. Candidate answer (CONJECTURAL)
Take γ to be a curve around the two critical values {a_1, v} with the "3/0 split" of background item (6). Then T_γ lifts to a twist that is trivial relative to A, so T_γ ∈ G. Concrete choice: γ = T_β²(γ0), where
- γ0 is the cusp curve at t=1/2 (background item (4));
- β is any curve around {v, a_0}, so T_β² ∈ G by item (5).

Then T_γ = T_β² T_{γ0} T_β^{−2}. It preserves D_f and fixes the component T_β²·D_0.

Claimed but NOT proved: some component (equivalently, after conjugating, D_0) has an infinite ⟨T_γ⟩-orbit. By background item (7) this is the statement that no nonzero power of T_γ lies in K. In the quotient Q ≅ Z/2*Z/2*Z/2 of background item (8), this reduces to showing that a specific parabolic conjugate of ℓ̄_1 is not in the subgroup generated by the G_0-orbit of x̄_{1/2}. That needs the action of G_0 on Q, which I have not computed.

## Status
- Proved: the formula for u(t) and its fibres/ramification (§1).
- Sketched (one unchecked surjectivity lemma): the quotient F̄ cannot settle the {v,a_j} family (§2).
- Open: an explicit γ with a proof of an infinite orbit. Specifically, (i) whether some curve around {v,a_j} has no power of T_γ² in K; (ii) whether a 3/0 curve around {a_1,v} such as T_β²(γ0) has an infinite orbit.

=== END OF ANSWER round2_q3 ===
=== Q4
# round2_q4 — answer (partial)

## Candidate curve
Use the normalization of background item (2) with a real parameter t in (1/2, (3-sqrt5)/2)... actually any fixed base point t_0 in W. Let gamma be a simple closed curve that bounds a disk Delta with Delta ∩ B = {a_1 = ∞, v}, i.e. it separates the two critical values {a_1, v} from {a_0, a_2, a_3}, and that is **not** in the G_0-orbit of the cusp curve gamma_0 at t = 1/2. Take k = 1 if gamma has the 3/0 split of item (6) (e.g. gamma = h(gamma_0) with h in G \ G_0), and note that for a 2/1-split curve no power lies in G, so only 3/0 curves can be candidates. Alternatively a curve around {v, a_j}, j in {0,2,3}, with k = 2 (item (5)).

## What is proved here
1. (Item (5), checked) For any gamma around {v, a_j}, j ∈ {0,2,3}: f^{-1}(Delta) is a single disk branched at c_2 containing only a_{j-1} from A, so T_gamma^2 lifts to the twist about a curve peripheral rel A, and i(T_gamma) = 1. Hence T_gamma^2 ∈ G and preserves D_f.
2. (Item (6), checked) For gamma around {a_1, v} with 3/0 split, T_gamma lifts to T_{δ1}T_{δ2} with δ_1 bounding a disk containing a_1,a_2,a_3 (and δ_2 bounding a disk with no point of A, hence trivial rel A), so the lift is trivial rel A... together with i(T_gamma)=1 this gives T_gamma ∈ G, so T_gamma preserves D_f.
3. Orbit is infinite iff no T_gamma^{kn} (n≠0) lies in K = G_0 ∩ F (item (7)).

## What is NOT proved (open)
I could not establish, for any explicit gamma, that T_gamma^{kn} ∉ K for all n ≠ 0. The abelian obstruction fails (item (3)); the quotient Q = F/<<ℓ_0²,ℓ_2²,ℓ_3²>> kills T_gamma^2 for the {v,a_j} curves, and for 3/0 curves around {a_1,v} the image in Q is a parabolic conjugate of ℓ_1, which may lie in the image of K, so Q does not decide it either. From memory (not verified) Hironaka–Koch (J. Mod. Dyn. 2017) prove the infinite orbit for a twist of this kind; I cannot reproduce their argument. The headline claim remains OPEN in this file.

## Shared background (results of an earlier round; items marked PROVED were checked, items marked "to be justified" are standard but must be argued if you use them)

Notation. The 4-cycle is a_0 = c_1, a_1 = f(c_1), a_2 = f(a_1), a_3 = f(a_2), f(a_3) = a_0. A = {a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3}, B = A ∪ {v}, v = f(c_2). The critical values are a_1 and v. Teich(B) has complex dimension 2, Teich(A) dimension 1, D_f dimension 1. i : PMod(S^2,B) → PMod(S^2,A) forgets v; its kernel is the point-pushing subgroup F := π_1(S^2∖A, v) ≅ F_3 (Birman exact sequence; PMod(S^2,A) ≅ π_1(M_{0,4}) is free of rank 2).

(1) Lifting framework (to be justified). If φ ∈ PMod(S^2,B) has a lift φ~ (f∘φ~ = φ∘f) fixing A pointwise, then f^*(φ·τ) = φ~·f^*(τ) and i_*(φ·τ) = i(φ)·i_*(τ). Let G = {φ : some such lift has φ~ = i(φ) in PMod(S^2,A)}; G preserves D_f. Conversely if τ and φ·τ both lie in D_f then φ ∈ G (both markings conjugate f to the same rational map). So with W := image of D_f in M_{0,5}, D_f/G ≅ W, G permutes the components transitively, and if D_0 is a component with stabilizer G_0 then π_0(D_f) ≅ G/G_0 and G_0 = image of the monodromy π_1(W) → π_1(M_{0,5}) = PMod(S^2,B) (D_0 → W is a covering since PMod(S^2,B) acts freely). The ⟨φ⟩-orbit of D_0 is infinite iff no nonzero power of φ lies in G_0. (Since degree 2 and the two critical values a_1, v are both marked, every φ ∈ PMod(S^2,B) lifts, uniquely up to the deck involution.)

(2) Explicit model (PROVED by direct computation, rechecked symbolically). Normalize a_0 = 0, a_1 = ∞, a_2 = 1, a_3 = t. Then
   f_t(z) = 1 + β/z + γ/z²,  β = (t²+t−1)/(1−t),  γ = t(1−2t)/(1−t),
   c_2 = −2γ/β,  and with D = 4t(1−2t)(1−t):
   v = −(t²−3t+1)²/D,   v−1 = −(t²+t−1)²/D,   v−t = −(3t²−3t+1)²/D.
The Möbius freedom is used up, so W ≅ C∖{0, 1, 1/2, roots of t²−3t+1, roots of t²+t−1, roots of 3t²−3t+1} (the t-sphere minus 10 points, counting ∞), embedded in M_{0,5} by t ↦ (a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3,v) = (0,∞,1,t,v(t)). Punctures:
   - roots of t²−3t+1: v → a_0 with contact order 2 (v − 0 vanishes to order 2);
   - roots of t²+t−1: v → a_2 = 1, order 2 (here β = 0, c_2 = ∞ = a_1);
   - roots of 3t²−3t+1: v → a_3 = t, order 2;
   - t = 1/2: γ = 0, f degenerates to the Möbius map 1 − 1/(2z) (which still has the 4-cycle 0→∞→1→1/2→0), c_2 → c_1 = 0 and v → ∞ = a_1 with a simple pole, while a_0,a_2,a_3 stay distinct;
   - t = 0: a_3 → a_0 and simultaneously v → a_1 (simple pole);  t = 1: a_3 → a_2 and v → a_1;  t = ∞: a_3 → a_1 and v → a_1 (v ~ t/8).
In terms of winding numbers of (t, t−1, v, v−1, v−t) the small loops around the punctures have classes: t=0: (1,0,−1,−1,−1); t=1: (0,1,−1,−1,−1); t=1/2: (0,0,−1,−1,−1); t=∞: (−1,−1,−1,−1,−1); each root of t²−3t+1: (0,0,2,0,0); of t²+t−1: (0,0,0,2,0); of 3t²−3t+1: (0,0,0,0,2).

(3) Abelian obstruction FAILS (PROVED). These vectors span a rank-5 sublattice of H_1(M_{0,5}) ≅ Z^5, so for every curve γ some power of [T_γ] lies in the image of H_1(W). A non-abelian invariant is needed.

(4) Cusp monodromies lie in G_0 (consequence of (2); the monodromy of a small loop around a puncture where two marked points collide with contact order m, the others staying apart, is T_c^{±m} for the curve c surrounding the colliding pair "along the short segment" in that configuration, transported to the base point):
   - for each of the 6 roots: the square of a twist about a specific curve around {v, a_j}, j ∈ {0,2,3} (two specific curves for each j);
   - for t = 1/2: a SINGLE twist T_{γ0}^{±1} about a specific curve γ0 surrounding the two critical values {a_1, v}.
   Hence these particular curves have FINITE (indeed trivial on D_0) orbits; a candidate answer must avoid being (up to G_0-conjugacy, with a power) one of them. Note G_0 depends on the component: the stabilizer of h·D_0 is h G_0 h^{-1}.

(5) Curves around {v, a_j}, j ∈ {0,2,3} (PROVED). If γ bounds a disk Δ with Δ ∩ B = {v, a_j}, Δ contains exactly one critical value, so f^{-1}(Δ) is one disk Δ~ (2:1, branched at c_2) and δ = ∂Δ~ = f^{-1}(γ) maps with degree 2; Δ~ ∩ A = {a_{j−1}} only (the other preimage of a_j and c_2 are not in A), so δ is peripheral rel A. T_γ^2 lifts to T_δ (trivial rel A) and i(T_γ) is trivial (i(γ) surrounds one point of A). Hence T_γ^2 ∈ G for EVERY such curve, whatever arc it follows. In F ≅ π_1(S^2∖A, v), T_γ is the point-push of v around a_j along the arc, i.e. a conjugate of the generator loop around a_j; T_γ^2 is a conjugate of its square.

(6) Curves around {a_1, v} (PROVED). If Δ ∩ B = {a_1, v}, then f^{-1}(Δ) is an annulus containing c_1 = a_0 and c_2, and the complementary disk Δ' (containing a_0,a_2,a_3) has preimage two disks E_1, E_2 mapped homeomorphically, δ_i = ∂E_i, each of degree 1; T_γ lifts to T_{δ_1}T_{δ_2}, and i(T_γ) = 1. The six points of f^{-1}({a_0,a_2,a_3}) ∖ … namely a_3,a_1,a_2 (in A) and their partners a_3',a_1',a_2' (not in A) split one of each pair into each E_i. If E_1 ⊃ {a_1,a_2,a_3} ("3/0 split") then T_γ ∈ G; if the split is 2/1 then no nonzero power of T_γ is in G. Since T_{γ0} ∈ G_0 ⊂ G by (4), γ0 has the 3/0 split, so 3/0 curves exist; any curve h(γ0), h ∈ G, is again 3/0 and T_{h(γ0)} = h T_{γ0} h^{-1} fixes the component h·D_0 — but it may still move D_0 with infinite orbit (the problem only asks for SOME infinite orbit).

(7) Reduction to point-pushes (planner's derivation; to be checked). The composite W → M_{0,5} → M_{0,4} (forget v) is t ↦ t, the inclusion of W into C∖{0,1}, which is surjective on π_1. Hence i(G_0) = PMod(S^2,A) ⊇ i(G), so G = G_0·H with H := G ∩ F, and π_0(D_f) ≅ G/G_0 ≅ H/K with K := G_0 ∩ F. Moreover K = image of N, where N ⊂ π_1(W) is the kernel of π_1(W) → π_1(C∖{0,1}), i.e. the normal closure of the small loops around the 7 extra punctures (t = 1/2 and the six roots). Thus K is generated by the G_0-conjugates of 7 elements of F: x_{1/2} (a conjugate in F of the loop ℓ_1 around a_1) and, for each j ∈ {0,2,3}, two elements that are conjugates of ℓ_j² (ℓ_j = loop around a_j). G_0 acts on F by conjugation inside PMod(S^2,B), i.e. by automorphisms each sending every ℓ_j to a conjugate of itself. A twist T_γ as in (5) or (6) lies in F; the question "no nonzero power of T_γ^k lies in G_0" becomes "no nonzero power of T_γ^k lies in K".
   Equivalent fibered picture: D_f → Teich(A) ≅ upper half plane; over τ_A the fiber is an H-torsor of lifts of v(t) to the universal cover of S^2∖A, and the component D_0 meets it in one K-orbit.

(8) A quotient worth exploiting. In Q := F/⟨⟨ℓ_0², ℓ_2², ℓ_3²⟩⟩ ≅ Z/2 * Z/2 * Z/2 (the orbifold fundamental group of the sphere with cone points of order 2 at a_0,a_2,a_3 and a cusp at a_1; the image of ℓ_1 is parabolic), the six root-type generators of K die, so the image of K in Q is generated by the images of the G_0-orbit of x_{1/2}, all parabolic conjugates of the image of ℓ_1. The G_0-action descends to Q. For a curve γ around {a_1, v} with 3/0 split, T_γ maps to a parabolic conjugate of ℓ_1 in Q. Analogously F/⟨⟨ℓ_1⟩⟩ ≅ π_1(S^2∖{a_0,a_2,a_3}) ≅ F_2 kills x_{1/2} and is the natural quotient for the {v,a_j} curves.

Check and write out every step of the sketch below in full: (a) the Teichmüller-theoretic setup (definition of f^* via pulling back the marked complex structure and restricting to A ⊂ f^{-1}(B); why D_f = Ψ^{-1}(diagonal); the fibration of Teich(B) over Teich(A) and the identification of point pushes with deck transformations of the fibre); (b) the algebra of Step 1 (derive V_t, the deck group, the fibres; explain precisely why, on the fibre over p0, f^* is the lift of the w-coordinate, including why the marked preimages follow the sheet continuously and why the base point τ ∈ D_f sits at w = t0); (c) Steps 2–3 (graphs, disjointness from Ψ(Teich(B)), the linking-number argument — be careful that the homotopy between Ψσ and Ψσ' really stays inside X_g); (d) Step 4 (the lift of β to H via λ; the identification g = T^{±2}S; non-ellipticity).

12	Notation. a_0 = c_1, a_{i+1} = f(a_i) (indices mod 4), A = {a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3}, B = A ∪ {v}, v = f(c_2). Problem statement (verbatim, for reference):
Let $f:\S^2\to \S^2$ be a branched cover, $V(f)$ be the set of its critical values,  and $A, B\subset \S^2$ be  finite sets.  \begin{enumerate} \item If $f(A)\cup V(f)\subset B$, then every complex structure on $(\S^2, B)$ can be pulled back to a complex structure on $(\S^2, A)$, and this induces the map  $f^*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.  \item If $A\subset B$, then forgetting the points $B\backslash A$ induces the map $i_*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.   \end{enumerate} If $f(A)\cup V(f)\cup A\subset B,$ then the deformation space is defined by $$\D_f:=\{\tau\in \Teich(B): f^*(\tau)=i_*(\tau)\}.$$ Consider a quadratic rational map $f$ with critical points $c_1$ and $c_2$. Assume that  $c_1$ belongs to a cycle of length $4$, and the critical value $v=f(c_2)$ does not belong to the cycle. By taking  $$A=\{c_1, f(c_1), f^{\circ 2}(c_1), f^{\circ 3}(c_1)\}, \quad B=A\cup \{v\},$$ we get a deformation space $\D_f\subset \Teich(B)$. Its image in the moduli space is the set of conjugacy classes of quadratic rational maps with the properties described above.  Explicitly describe a simple closed curve $\gamma\subset (\S^2, B)$ such that a power of the Dehn twist around this curve preserves the deformation space, and its action on the set of connected components of $\D_f$ has an infinite orbit.

Problem statement (verbatim, for reference):
Let $f:\S^2\to \S^2$ be a branched cover, $V(f)$ be the set of its critical values,  and $A, B\subset \S^2$ be  finite sets.  \begin{enumerate} \item If $f(A)\cup V(f)\subset B$, then every complex structure on $(\S^2, B)$ can be pulled back to a complex structure on $(\S^2, A)$, and this induces the map  $f^*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.  \item If $A\subset B$, then forgetting the points $B\backslash A$ induces the map $i_*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.   \end{enumerate} If $f(A)\cup V(f)\cup A\subset B,$ then the deformation space is defined by $$\D_f:=\{\tau\in \Teich(B): f^*(\tau)=i_*(\tau)\}.$$ Consider a quadratic rational map $f$ with critical points $c_1$ and $c_2$. Assume that  $c_1$ belongs to a cycle of length $4$, and the critical value $v=f(c_2)$ does not belong to the cycle. By taking  $$A=\{c_1, f(c_1), f^{\circ 2}(c_1), f^{\circ 3}(c_1)\}, \quad B=A\cup \{v\},$$ we get a deformation space $\D_f\subset \Teich(B)$. Its image in the moduli space is the set of conjugacy classes of quadratic rational maps with the properties described above.  Explicitly describe a simple closed curve $\gamma\subset (\S^2, B)$ such that a power of the Dehn twist around this curve preserves the deformation space, and its action on the set of connected components of $\D_f$ has an infinite orbit.

# Answer to round3_q3

## Status
- **Checked by hand:** the Step 0 normal form (f_t(0)=∞, f_t(∞)=1, f_t(1)=t, f_t(t)=0; at t=1/4: β=−11/12, γ=1/6, c_2=4/11, v=−25/96), and V_t(t)=v(t).
- **Proved, given Step 1:** the topological criterion (Steps 2–3) and its use for the twist T_γ (Step 4).
- **Not proved, only numerically supported (planner's numerics, which I have not re-checked):** that the explicit arc α=V_{1/4}∘β is simple, and the description of where it crosses the real axis.
- **Not done:** parts (1) (that Ψ is a covering onto U) and (3) (the k=2 family) of the query. The argument below does not need them; they remain open.

## Setting and normal form
Write a_0=c_1 and a_{i+1}=f(a_i). Normalize a_0=0, a_1=∞, a_2=1, a_3=t. Then
f_t(z)=1+β/z+γ/z², with β=(t²+t−1)/(1−t) and γ=t(1−2t)/(1−t).

Check:
- f_t has a double pole at 0, so c_1=0 is critical and f(a_0)=∞=a_1.
- f(∞)=1=a_2.
- f(1)=1+β+γ=1+(t−1)=t=a_3, because β+γ=−(1−t)²/(1−t)=t−1.
- f(t)=0=a_0, because t²+βt+γ=[t²(1−t)+t³+t²−t+t−2t²]/(1−t)=0.

At t=1/4: β=−11/12, γ=1/6, c_2=−2γ/β=4/11, and v=1−121/48+121/96=−25/96. On the real line the order is v<a_0=0<a_3=1/4<a_2=1, with a_1=∞.

## Step 1 (fibre model)
This step is taken from the planner and not re-derived here. Fix t, so the configuration A is (0,∞,1,t), and let the fifth point be v'. Then the pulled-back modulus of A is w, where
v' = V_t(w) = −((w−1)²−t)² / (4w(w−1)(w+t−1)).

- At w=t this gives −(t²−3t+1)²/D, with D=4t(1−2t)(1−t). This equals v(t), which I checked.
- The fibre of V_t over a_1=∞ is {0,1,∞,1−t}, and all four points are simple.
- Consequence: w≠1−t whenever v'≠a_1. So Ψ=(i_*,f^*) never meets the graphs Γ_g={(p,g(p))}, for g∈Γ(2)S, which lie over {q=1−t}.

## Step 2–3 (criterion), proved
Let g∈Γ(2)S be non-elliptic, i.e. it has no fixed point in H. Then Γ_g∩Δ=∅.

The space X_g=(H×H)∖Γ_g is homotopy equivalent to a circle, so H_1(X_g)=Z. The generator is a fibre loop around g(p), and the diagonal Δ≅H is contractible inside X_g.

Let T∈ker(i) satisfy f^*∘T=f^*. Then Ψ∘T=Ψ, so T preserves D_f=Ψ^{-1}(Δ). Suppose T^m fixes the component D_0 of D_f through τ, with m≠0.
1. Choose a path σ⊂D_0 from τ to T^mτ. Then Ψσ is a loop in Δ, so it is null-homologous in X_g.
2. Choose a path σ' in the fibre i_*^{-1}(p_0) with the same endpoints. Teich(B) is contractible, so σ≃σ' rel endpoints.
3. Ψ(Teich B)⊂X_g, so Ψσ and Ψσ' have the same class in H_1(X_g).
4. Ψσ' is a fibre loop. If it winds ±m times around g(p_0), this contradicts step 1.

So the ⟨T⟩-orbit of D_0 is infinite.

## Step 4 (the curve)
Fibre loop: let T be the point-push of v around the lasso α·(circle around a_1)·α^{-1}, where α is an arc from v to a_1. Then T=T_γ^{±1}, where γ=∂N(α) is the curve enclosing exactly {v,a_1}.

Lift α from w=t_0 to an arc β. If β ends at w=1−t_0, then the lasso lifts to a closed loop β·(circle around 1−t_0)·β^{-1}. This loop avoids 0, 1 and ∞, so it lifts through λ to a closed loop in H winding once around q*=g(p_0). Hence:
- **T preserves D_f.** f^*∘T=f^* on the fibre. The lift T~ fixes a point of Teich(A), and pure mapping classes act freely there, so T~ is trivial.
- **The orbit is infinite.** T^m winds m times around q*, so Step 3 applies as soon as g is not elliptic.

Choice at t_0=1/4: take β to be a loop around w=0 based at 1/4, followed by the segment [1/4,3/4].
- The loop around 0 lifts to a translation by ±2.
- The segment lifts along the imaginary axis to S(p_0).
- So g=τ↦±2−1/τ, which has trace ±2. It is parabolic, not elliptic, so the orbit is infinite.
- For contrast, the bare segment gives g=S, which is elliptic. That is the cusp curve at t=1/2, and its twist stabilizes a component.

An explicit β:
1. the lower half of |w|=1/4, from 1/4 to −1/4;
2. the upper half of |w−5/32|=13/32, from −1/4 to 9/16;
3. the lower half of |w−21/32|=3/32, from 9/16 to 3/4.

## Answer (for f=f_{1/4})
γ is the boundary of a thin regular neighbourhood of the arc α from v=−25/96 to a_1=f(c_1)=∞. The arc α:
1. starts at v and runs in the lower half-plane;
2. crosses the real axis upward in (a_2,a_1)=(1,∞);
3. runs in the upper half-plane and crosses downward in (a_0,a_3)=(0,1/4);
4. crosses upward in (v,a_0);
5. stays in the upper half-plane and goes to ∞.

So γ separates {v,a_1} from {a_0,a_2,a_3}. The twist T_γ itself (power 1) preserves D_f, and the ⟨T_γ⟩-orbit of the component through the base point is infinite. The proof of this is complete, apart from Step 1, which is the planner's computation, and the numerically supported claim that α is simple.

Open: rigorous simplicity of α, part (1) (the covering-map structure of Ψ), and part (3) (the k=2 family).

# Answer: an explicit twist curve with an infinite orbit on π_0(D_f)

The proof below is written for the base map f = f_{1/4}. The planner's sketch was checked step by step. Every algebraic identity it uses was re-derived by hand. The numerical claim that the arc is simple is replaced by an exact combinatorial argument (§4), using the fact that V^{-1}(real line) is the union of the real line and two explicit circles.

## 0. Setup, notation, standard facts (cited from memory)

a_0 = c_1, a_{i+1} = f(a_i) (indices mod 4), A = {a_0,…,a_3}, B = A ∪ {v}. The critical values are a_1 = f(c_1) and v. Teich(A) is identified with H, and the modulus map π: Teich(A) → C∖{0,1} is the coordinate t of the normalisation (a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3) ↦ (0,∞,1,t). We take π = λ, the modular lambda function: a universal covering H → C∖{0,1} with deck group Γ(2)/±1. Its standard properties are λ(τ+2) = λ(τ), λ(−1/τ) = 1−λ(τ), and λ ≈ 16e^{iπτ} as τ → i∞. In particular, λ maps iR_{>0} decreasingly onto (0,1).

**Bers/Birman fibration (from memory).** i_*: Teich(B) → Teich(A) is a fibration. The fibre over p is the universal cover of S²∖A_p (A_p is the configuration with modulus π(p)), parametrised by the position v' of the fifth point. The point-push subgroup ker(PMod(S²,B) → PMod(S²,A)) ≅ π_1(S²∖A, v) acts on each fibre as its deck group. Teich(B) is contractible.

**Pullback.** f^*(τ) is the pullback of the marked structure, restricted to A ⊂ f^{-1}(B). For φ ∈ PMod(S²,B) there is a lift φ~ with f∘φ~ = φ∘f, and f^*(φτ) = φ~·f^*(τ). Similarly, i_*(φτ) = i(φ)·i_*(τ).

Put Ψ = (i_*, f^*): Teich(B) → H×H. Then D_f = Ψ^{-1}(Δ), where Δ is the diagonal.

## 1. Explicit model (verified by hand)

Normalise a_0 = 0, a_1 = ∞, a_2 = 1, a_3 = t, and put f_t(z) = 1 + b/z + c/z², with b = (t²+t−1)/(1−t) and c = t(1−2t)/(1−t). Then:
- 0 is a critical point mapping to ∞ (double pole), and f(∞) = 1.
- f(1) = 1+b+c = t, because b + c = −(1−t)²/(1−t) = t−1.
- f(t) = 0 ⇔ t² + bt + c = 0. The numerator is t²(1−t) + t(t²+t−1) + t(1−2t) = 0.

At t0 = 1/4 this gives b = −11/12, c = 1/6, c_2 = −2c/b = 4/11, and v = 1 − 121/48 + 121/96 = −25/96. On the real line the order is v < a_0 = 0 < a_3 = 1/4 < a_2 = 1 < a_1 = ∞.

## 2. The fibrewise formula (Step 1, verified)

Fix t and let v' ∉ {0,1,t,∞}. Up to Möbius maps, the pullback of (Ĉ; 0,∞,1,t,v') is given by F(z) = v' + z², whose critical points are ∞ ↦ ∞ = a_1 and 0 ↦ v'. The marked preimages are:
- a_0' = ∞;
- a_1' = s_2 with s_2² = 1−v' (a preimage of a_2);
- a_2' = s_3 with s_3² = t−v' (a preimage of a_3);

Let $f:\S^2\to \S^2$ be a branched cover, $V(f)$ be the set of its critical values,  and $A, B\subset \S^2$ be  finite sets.  \begin{enumerate} \item If $f(A)\cup V(f)\subset B$, then every complex structure on $(\S^2, B)$ can be pulled back to a complex structure on $(\S^2, A)$, and this induces the map  $f^*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.  \item If $A\subset B$, then forgetting the points $B\backslash A$ induces the map $i_*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.   \end{enumerate} If $f(A)\cup V(f)\cup A\subset B,$ then the deformation space is defined by $$\D_f:=\{\tau\in \Teich(B): f^*(\tau)=i_*(\tau)\}.$$ Consider a quadratic rational map $f$ with critical points $c_1$ and $c_2$. Assume that  $c_1$ belongs to a cycle of length $4$, and the critical value $v=f(c_2)$ does not belong to the cycle. By taking  $$A=\{c_1, f(c_1), f^{\circ 2}(c_1), f^{\circ 3}(c_1)\}, \quad B=A\cup \{v\},$$ we get a deformation space $\D_f\subset \Teich(B)$. Its image in the moduli space is the set of conjugacy classes of quadratic rational maps with the properties described above.  Explicitly describe a simple closed curve $\gamma\subset (\S^2, B)$ such that a power of the Dehn twist around this curve preserves the deformation space, and its action on the set of connected components of $\D_f$ has an infinite orbit.

Let $f:\S^2\to \S^2$ be a branched cover, $V(f)$ be the set of its critical values,  and $A, B\subset \S^2$ be  finite sets.  \begin{enumerate} \item If $f(A)\cup V(f)\subset B$, then every complex structure on $(\S^2, B)$ can be pulled back to a complex structure on $(\S^2, A)$, and this induces the map  $f^*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.  \item If $A\subset B$, then forgetting the points $B\backslash A$ induces the map $i_*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.   \end{enumerate} If $f(A)\cup V(f)\cup A\subset B,$ then the deformation space is defined by $$\D_f:=\{\tau\in \Teich(B): f^*(\tau)=i_*(\tau)\}.$$ Consider a quadratic rational map $f$ with critical points $c_1$ and $c_2$. Assume that  $c_1$ belongs to a cycle of length $4$, and the critical value $v=f(c_2)$ does not belong to the cycle. By taking  $$A=\{c_1, f(c_1), f^{\circ 2}(c_1), f^{\circ 3}(c_1)\}, \quad B=A\cup \{v\},$$ we get a deformation space $\D_f\subset \Teich(B)$. Its image in the moduli space is the set of conjugacy classes of quadratic rational maps with the properties described above.  Explicitly describe a simple closed curve $\gamma\subset (\S^2, B)$ such that a power of the Dehn twist around this curve preserves the deformation space, and its action on the set of connected components of $\D_f$ has an infinite orbit.

Problem statement (for reference — /data/output/logs/prob-007/work/math-proof-run/problem.md is the authoritative text; go by the file wherever this copy differs or looks garbled):
Let $f:\S^2\to \S^2$ be a branched cover, $V(f)$ be the set of its critical values,  and $A, B\subset \S^2$ be  finite sets.  \begin{enumerate} \item If $f(A)\cup V(f)\subset B$, then every complex structure on $(\S^2, B)$ can be pulled back to a complex structure on $(\S^2, A)$, and this induces the map  $f^*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.  \item If $A\subset B$, then forgetting the points $B\backslash A$ induces the map $i_*:\Teich(B)\to \Teich(A)$.   \end{enumerate} If $f(A)\cup V(f)\cup A\subset B,$ then the deformation space is defined by $$\D_f:=\{\tau\in \Teich(B): f^*(\tau)=i_*(\tau)\}.$$ Consider a quadratic rational map $f$ with critical points $c_1$ and $c_2$. Assume that  $c_1$ belongs to a cycle of length $4$, and the critical value $v=f(c_2)$ does not belong to the cycle. By taking  $$A=\{c_1, f(c_1), f^{\circ 2}(c_1), f^{\circ 3}(c_1)\}, \quad B=A\cup \{v\},$$ we get a deformation space $\D_f\subset \Teich(B)$. Its image in the moduli space is the set of conjugacy classes of quadratic rational maps with the properties described above.  Explicitly describe a simple closed curve $\gamma\subset (\S^2, B)$ such that a power of the Dehn twist around this curve preserves the deformation space, and its action on the set of connected components of $\D_f$ has an infinite orbit.
